Texan here.

For those that don't know, here is how Texas energy works:

Electricity services are split into 3 services, and each company must only belong to one group. These groups are Generators, Transmitters, and Billers/Resellers.

Generators run, well, the generators! So, the actual physical plants where the turbines spin to create electricity.

Transmitters operate and must maintain the physical lines from the generating plant to the end consumer, including transformers. They are responsible for the cost of all storm repair, and day to day issues of individual homes and businesses needing power connected and operating.

Retail/resellers are the only ones who can deal directly with consumers. They can set prices, etc. and their responsibility is to collect the monies form the end consumer AND to pay the transmitters and generators.

The generators get a set price (set every year) for each KW/H sold. The transmitters get a set price per KW/H sold. The resllers collect any amount sold over the set costs of the generator and the transmitter. for example, for every KW/H sold, the generator will get 5.6 cents, and the transmitter will get 3.698 cents.If they sold you at $11.7 cents per KW/H, then the generator gets their 5.6 cents, the transmitter gets their 3.698 cents, and the reseller gets 2.4 cents per Kw/H.

Now, to this bill. Tjis bill is ONLY for the transmitter side - the one responsible for all the connections between the power plant and the end user. They are also responsible for all repairs, storm cleanup, and new lines. They are responsible for making sure the transformers, poles, and lines are working, clear of debris or fire hazards (see PG&E), and keeping the grid operational.

The USA has 3 power grids - Eastern US, Western US, and Texas. (I shit you not, Texas has it's own power grid.) What this bill is saying is that any company who wants to be a transmitter (owns, operates, and maintains the lines and grid, must be approved by the state. After Hurricane Ike, many of these small transmitters went bankrupt because they couldn't pay for the storm cleanup. We had a 2 cents a Kw/H surcharge added to our electric bill for 7 years to pay back Centerpoint for doing the cleanup these other companies couldn't do, because they couldn't pay for it. That's about a 20-25% additional cost added to every customer due to companies not being solvent enough to maintain the grid.

In addition, the cleanup took over 2 weeks in many parts of Houston. 2 weeks, no power for much of the 4th largest city.

So, as a Texan, this bill protects me, and if fly-by-night companies can't come in, payoff some local mayor or council to get their service in, and then when the next storm hits, I'm fucked with no power for 2 weeks again, AND I have to pay 20-25% higher bills for 7 years? Yeah, I'm OK with this.
